01.r: No father is recorded for him.
01.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'fatherless', and for this verse 'without father, i.e., with no recorded genealogy'. On that reading the point is the silence of the record, not a claim about his birth. This verse is the word's only New Testament use.

02.r: No mother is recorded for him.
02.n: Abbott-Smith notes that Greek writers often used the word of the gods, and that here, paired with 'without father', it describes one without recorded genealogy.

03.r: No line of descent is recorded for him.
03.n: Abbott-Smith explains it as 'without recorded pedigree' and derives it from the verb rendered 'whose descent is traced' in Hebrews 7:6. It matters because the Levitical priests held office by descent.

04.r: Opens a pair of denials: neither this nor that.

05.r: A starting point to his days.

09.r: A recorded end to his life.
09.n: This is τέλος, the word this study renders 'toll' where it means a payment. Here it has its first sense in Abbott-Smith, 'end', the limit of a state, and has nothing to do with money.

10.r: Present participle: he has neither the one nor the other.

11.r: He has been made to resemble the Son of God.
11.n: A perfect passive participle, 'having been made like'; Abbott-Smith gives 'to make like' with this passive use as its only New Testament occurrence. The grammar runs from Melchizedek to the Son: he is made like the Son, not the Son like him.

12.r: Turns from what he lacks to what he is.

14.r: The Son of God, the subject of the letter.

15.r: The article with 'God'; English does not use it.

17.r: Present tense: he goes on being a priest.
17.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to stay, abide, remain'. The verb has no stated subject; 'he' is Melchizedek, carried over from the verses before.

19.r: Part of the phrase 'continually'; it has no English of its own here.

20.r: Part of the phrase 'continually'; it has no English of its own here.

21.r: His priesthood runs on without interruption.
21.n: Literally 'into the unbroken'. Abbott-Smith gives the adjective as 'unbroken, continuous', and the phrase εἰς τὸ διηνεκές adverbially as 'continually', citing this verse. The Geneva and DRC's 'for ever' goes a step beyond the word's own sense, which is that there is no break.
